patella.summary: The largest sesamoid bone in the body. It develops in the tendon of quadriceps femoris and lies in front of the knee joint.
facts: Sesamoid bone
Base (top), apex (bottom), articular surface (back; the lateral facet is larger)
Quadriceps tendon above, patellar ligament below (to the tibial tuberosity)
Lengthens the lever arm of quadriceps and so increases extension force; protects the femoral condyles
clinical: As the Q angle increases (usually in women) the patella tends to dislocate laterally; the lower fibres of vastus medialis resist this.
Patellar fractures result from direct blows; the integrity of the extensor mechanism must be checked.
The patellar (knee-jerk) reflex tests segments L2–L4 (especially L4).
tus: The largest sesamoid bone in the body; it develops in the quadriceps tendon.
A bipartite patella is usually at the upper outer corner and must not be mistaken for a fracture.

tibia.summary: The large, weight-bearing bone on the medial side of the leg. Its anterior border can be felt under the skin along its whole length.
facts: Long bone
Medial and lateral condyles, intercondylar eminence, tibial tuberosity, fibular articular facet
Anterior border (shin), medial surface (subcutaneous), soleal line
Medial malleolus, fibular notch, inferior articular surface
Femur (knee), fibula (proximal and distal tibiofibular joints), talus (ankle)
clinical: The tibial shaft is the long bone most often fractured open; its anteromedial surface is covered only by skin and its poor blood supply slows healing.
Shin splints are common in runners.
In adolescents a painful swelling at the tibial tuberosity is Osgood–Schlatter disease.
tus: The front of the tibia lies under the skin; open fractures are commonest in this bone.
Compartment syndrome is an important complication of tibial fractures.

fibula.summary: The slender long bone on the lateral side of the leg. It carries no body weight; it gives attachment to muscles and joins the ankle by forming the lateral malleolus.
facts: Long bone
Head (apex), neck, shaft, lateral malleolus
Tibia (tibiofibular joint, tibiofibular syndesmosis), talus
Biceps femoris, fibular muscles, extensor digitorum longus, extensor hallucis longus, soleus, tibialis posterior, flexor hallucis longus
clinical: The common fibular nerve wrapping around the fibular neck can be damaged by a blow or a tight cast; foot drop results.
The middle of the fibular shaft can be harvested as a vascularised bone graft.
Fractures of the lateral malleolus are common in ankle sprains.
tus: The fibula carries no body weight; the free fibula flap is used to reconstruct the mandible.
Maisonneuve fracture: deltoid ligament tear + syndesmosis injury + proximal fibular fracture.

talus.summary: The bone that transfers weight between the leg bones and the foot and forms the lower part of the ankle joint. No muscle attaches to it.
facts: Head, neck, body, trochlea, lateral and posterior processes
Tibia and fibula (ankle joint), calcaneus (subtalar joint), navicular (talocalcaneonavicular joint)
Most of its surface is covered by articular cartilage; no muscle attaches
clinical: Fractures of the talar neck (aviator's fracture) can lead to avascular necrosis because the blood supply is disrupted.
tus: The risk of AVN after talar neck fractures is graded with the Hawkins classification.
The upper surface of the talus (trochlea) is wider in front; the ankle is most stable in dorsiflexion.

calcaneus.summary: The largest bone of the foot. It forms the heel and transmits weight to the ground when standing.
facts: Calcaneal tuberosity, sustentaculum tali, groove for the flexor hallucis longus tendon, fibular trochlea
Talus (subtalar joint), cuboid (calcaneocuboid joint)
Calcaneal (Achilles) tendon, plantar aponeurosis, flexor digitorum brevis, abductor hallucis, abductor digiti minimi, quadratus plantae, extensor digitorum brevis
clinical: The calcaneus breaks in a fall from a height onto the feet; the spine must also be checked because a vertebral compression fracture may accompany it.
A heel spur (calcaneal spur) and plantar fasciitis are common causes of heel pain.
tus: The most frequently fractured tarsal bone; a lumbar compression fracture may accompany a fall from a height.
The Achilles tendon attaches to the calcaneal tuberosity; a reduced Böhler angle indicates a fracture.

os-naviculare.summary: A boat-shaped bone on the medial side of the foot between the talus and the cuneiforms. It is the keystone of the medial arch.
facts: Navicular tuberosity (main attachment of tibialis posterior)
Talus, the three cuneiforms, sometimes the cuboid
clinical: An accessory navicular bone can form a painful bump on the medial border of the foot.
Köhler disease is avascular necrosis of the navicular in children.
tus: An accessory navicular can cause pain in the tibialis posterior tendon.
Köhler disease is osteonecrosis of the navicular in children.

os-cuboideum.summary: A cube-shaped bone on the lateral side of the foot between the calcaneus and the 4th and 5th metatarsals.
facts: Cuboid tuberosity, groove for the fibularis longus tendon
Calcaneus, lateral cuneiform, navicular, 4th and 5th metatarsals
tus: The cuboid is the keystone of the lateral longitudinal arch; the fibularis longus tendon passes beneath it.

ossa-cuneiformia.summary: Three wedge-shaped bones between the navicular and the first three metatarsals: medial, intermediate and lateral.
facts: Medial cuneiform (largest), intermediate (smallest), lateral
Navicular, 1st–3rd metatarsals, cuboid (lateral cuneiform)
Their wedge shapes help form the transverse arch of the foot
tus: Tibialis anterior and fibularis longus both attach to the medial cuneiform and base of the 1st metatarsal (the 'stirrup').

ossa-metatarsi.summary: The five long bones forming the skeleton of the forefoot. The first is the shortest and thickest; their heads carry much of the weight when standing.
facts: Tuberosity of the 5th metatarsal at its base (fibularis brevis attaches); two sesamoid bones under the head of the 1st metatarsal
Tarsometatarsal joints (Lisfranc joint), metatarsophalangeal joints
clinical: Fracture of the base of the 5th metatarsal (Jones fracture) is common in ankle sprains.
Stress fractures of the 2nd–3rd metatarsals (march fracture) can follow long marches.
In hallux valgus the 1st metatarsal deviates medially and the big toe laterally.
tus: A march fracture is most often a stress fracture of the shaft of the 2nd metatarsal.
A Lisfranc injury involves the tarsometatarsal joint complex; the base of the 2nd metatarsal is the keystone.

phalanges-pedis.summary: The 14 bones of the toes. The big toe (hallux) has two phalanges, the other toes three each; they are shorter than those of the hand.
facts: Metatarsophalangeal and interphalangeal joints of the foot
Two sesamoid bones lie under the metatarsophalangeal joint of the hallux
clinical: Hammer toe deformity and gouty arthritis (especially of the 1st MTP joint – podagra) are common problems.
tus: Hallux valgus is lateral deviation of the big toe; a bunion develops over the head of the 1st metatarsal.
